🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -2.02% (intraday, 7-year +29bp). At trading day 19 (last close) it was -1.10% against a five-campaign average of -1.19% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.35%. The 10-year is +30bp since the hike vs a +16bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 3 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 719bp against a five-year average of 411bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +40bp and BB +35bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.31 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • Bank Earnings: 3 banks reported (BAC, MS, STT); no red flags. Credit broadly stable; deposit costs flat.
  • Stocks: US stock futures point lower; Nasdaq futures lead the drop, Europe edges higher.
  • FX: Dollar strengthens broadly; the euro is well below its long-term average price.
  • Technicals: US stocks remain unusually stretched above their averages; gold and the euro are trending down.
  • Sectors: Energy keeps leading; tech cooled this week; banks have lagged this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lowest-rated junk bonds are under real strain; it's spreading, slowly, to stronger borrowers.
  • Crisis: Moderate overall stress; biggest risks are oil and the weakest junk borrowers.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is easing, but nearly 3 in 10 prices still rise fast.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are far below 2000 extremes, but credit and volatility look complacent.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Meta is the biggest reporter; Lam Research has the biggest expected move.
  • Iran: No verifiable update for today; last confirmed reports are months old.
  • Warsh: Warsh is leaning hawkish; a hike stays possible at the Oct 28 meeting.
  • Outlook: Cautious near term: rising yields and junk stress offset firm stock trends.
  • Trades: Upgrade junk quality, stay long energy, short the euro, hedge stocks.

The biggest story this morning is rates. The US 2Y is at 4.9478%, up 0.1588 from 4.789%, and the 10Y is at 5.3229%, up 0.1145. The front end is leading, so the computed 2s10s is down to 37.94 bp: a hawkish bear-flattener. That is consistent with markets repricing toward a Warsh Fed that has kept a hike on the table for the October 28 FOMC (see Warsh section; we could not verify any specific catalyst today). Ten-year note futures are down 0.609375 to 104.125. Equity futures are soft vs the prior session: ES is 7837.5 (-18.25), NQ is 30632.75 (-158.75) and Dow futures are 51852 (-83). That follows a flat-to-lower cash close (SPX 7805.45, -0.02%; RTY -0.40%) with the VIX at 15.8, up from 15.27. The dollar is firm: DXY 102.625 (+0.445), EUR/USD 1.1123 vs 1.1199. Precious metals are being hit by higher real yields: gold is at 4089.53 (-71.21) and silver at 57.0644 (-2.0902). WTI is at 95.51 (+1.37) and Brent at 105.74. Europe is shrugging it off (SX5E +0.29%, STOXX 600 +0.35%). The under-the-surface story is junk contagion. The Caa–B OAS gap is 719 bp. That is the 100th percentile of the last 5 years and the widest since 2020-04-24, against a 5-year average near 411 bp. It is up 79 bp in a month and 202 bp in three. Caa OAS is 1017 bp, up 119 bp in a month. The stress is starting to leak up the ladder: single-B is +40 bp in a month (298 bp) and Ba +35 bp (189 bp). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen to 0.52 from 0.35 a month ago and 0.31 three months ago, though it is still below its 0.70 5-year median. The FRED ICE cross-check agrees: the CCC–B gap is 943 bp, the 100th percentile of its history. IG is barely moving (+3 bp in a month to 82 bp), and the B–Ba gap (109 bp) is below its 5-year average. So single-B and BB are widening together with the broader market, not breaking away. In short, the CCC rot is clearly intensifying and has begun dragging single-B and BB wider, but it has not yet reached investment grade. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Overall sentiment is cautious: stocks are near highs and still extended, but rates, the dollar and the bottom of the credit stack are all pushing the other way. Bank earnings today (BAC, MS, BLK, STT, PGR and FAST are scheduled for 2026-10-14) are the next test for financials, which are -3.66% over the past month.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Energy is the unambiguous leader. US Energy is +1.74% 1d, +5.58% 1w, +4.84% 1m and +47.09% YTD; global Energy is +1.83% 1d, +4.90% 1w and +40.64% YTD, tracking WTI near 95.5 and Brent above 105. This week's rotation has a defensive tilt. US Cons Staples is +3.25% 1w, Real Estate +1.70%, Utilities +1.67% and Health Care +1.56%. Info Tech is -2.32% 1w (global -3.70%) and Industrials -1.71% (global -1.97%). Tech is still the 1m leader (+6.34% US, +5.16% global) and has a big YTD lead (+28.73% US, +34.27% global), so this looks like profit-taking in growth rather than a regime break. Financials are the weak cyclical: US -3.66% 1m and -0.18% YTD, global -4.39% 1m. That is consistent with the junk-credit stress and a flattening curve, which squeezes lending margins, so today's bank earnings matter. Health Care fell -1.33% 1d (global -1.04%). Comm Services gained +0.88%. Net read: value/commodity cyclicals (Energy) plus defensives are beating growth and rate-sensitive cyclicals (Financials, Industrials, Real Estate 1m -2.42%). That is a late-cycle, inflation-hedge mix rather than a broad risk-on rotation.

The tails tell a different story. The Bloomberg Caa OAS is 1017 bp (+31 1w, +119 1m, +230 3m), the 96th percentile of 5 years. The Caa–B gap is 719 bp, the 100th percentile of 5 years and the widest since April 2020. FRED shows CCC at 1253 bp and CCC–B at 943 bp, both at the 100th percentile of history. Stress is migrating up: single-B is +40 bp in a month to 298 bp, Ba +35 bp to 189 bp, and HY–IG +39 bp to 231 bp. The Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen to 0.52 from 0.31 three months ago. IG is the firewall, at 82 bp and only +3 bp in a month. Key levels and what it would take to reach them (analyst framing, descriptive only): 1. **HY OAS to ~3.50%** (EUR HY's current level and roughly the Hike-2022 overlap zone): requires single-B to keep widening ~40 bp/month while CCC stays above 1000 bp. 2. **US IG to ~1.00–1.22%** (1.22 is the tech-bubble peak benchmark): would need contagion to cross into BBB. The trigger would most likely be a growth scare or a failed bank print, not just CCC idiosyncratic defaults. 3. **Reversal:** the Caa–B gap drifting back toward its ~411 bp 5-year average would require oil and front-end yields to stop rising.

Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.64 vol points (17th percentile of the 42 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.1 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 105bp (steeper by 29bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 77% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (84bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.32 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 77%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 13 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — The core trend is cooling but inflation is not finished. Every trimmed and sticky measure in the computed set is falling: median CPI 2.58, trimmed-mean CPI 2.57, median PCE 2.57, trimmed-mean PCE 2.19 and core sticky CPI 2.70. Their percentile ranks sit near the middle of history (49–65), and the separately rendered computed Core-Trend Sub-Score reflects that mid-range. Breadth is less benign. On the Dallas distribution, 13.2% of the PCE basket is running above 10% and 15.7% at 5–10%, so nearly 29% is inflating fast. Flexible CPI is 4.94%, in the 76th percentile. Headline-sensitive gauges stay hot: core PCE YoY 3.00759 and 1y breakeven 2.858 vs 5y 2.4018, an inverted breakeven curve. That says the market sees the energy-driven price pressure as near-term rather than embedded. Wages are not an accelerant (average hourly earnings 3.0, ECI 0.9). Analyst view: moderate persistence, with the risk skewed by oil.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (43x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Aggregate valuation is extreme (analyst estimates from web sources): Shiller CAPE is around 41.6, against a 44.19 dot-com monthly peak; market-cap/GDP is about 237%; top-10 concentration is roughly 35%. But the Nasdaq's own trailing P/E is nowhere near 2000 mania. This is concentration in profitable mega-caps rather than a speculative profitless-tech blowout. IPO froth is building, with Anthropic reportedly preparing a mega-listing and Jio Platforms and Firmus in the pipeline, but it is not yet at 1999 breadth (analyst estimate 55). Long-term EPS-growth expectations look elevated (analyst estimate 70), a BofA signpost to watch. The computed path chart has the current cycle (anchored Oct-2022) at month 48 at 247.6. That is roughly where the dot-com path from the 1990 low stood at month 48 (235.7), long before its month-113 peak. The analog says time remains, but the analog alone cannot time a top. What would turn this from 'expensive' to 'late': PMIs rolling over, NFCI tightening from -0.49 toward -0.15, and the CCC contagion reaching IG.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Oct 28 FOMC: analyst inference is a hawkish hold, with a live (minority) chance of a 25 bp hike. Warsh dropped forward guidance and has repeatedly said prices are too high, and at Jackson Hole he left a hike open. Today's +0.1588 jump in the 2Y to 4.9478% is consistent with markets leaning that way. We could not verify the September 16 outcome, so the current rate level is uncertain; sources cite a 3.5–3.75% range.

~1 YEAR

Analyst inference: a 'higher-for-longer, then normalize' path. That means 0–2 hikes if core PCE (3.00759) stalls near 3%, and no cuts until the underlying measures (now 2.2–2.7% and falling) convince him. Expect a structurally smaller balance sheet (QT bias) and reduced forward guidance, given his task forces on communications, the balance sheet and the inflation framework. This is inferred from his record, not from any stated plan.

On the record, Warsh has: - removed forward guidance at his June debut ('I can't give you any forward guidance about what we're going to do next'). The hold that meeting was the fourth in a row, and 9 of 18 dots penciled in a hike; - said at Sintra that 'prices are too high'; - recommitted at Jackson Hole to getting inflation back to 2% while leaving a hike open, which pushed market odds of a September hike to about 60%; - per a reported FT story, been prepared to hike in September if the data stayed hot. Trump has publicly pressed for lower rates but deferred the October decision to Warsh. Our inference: the computed core-trend disinflation gives him cover to hold, but oil-driven flexible inflation (4.94%) and core PCE near 3% keep a hike optionality he will not surrender. These sources are secondary and some conflict on inflation levels, so treat the details accordingly.
